title: Sony Pictures hack — the Guardians of Peace

scenes.label: A red skeleton on every screen
scenes.narration: [serious] It's Monday, November 24, 2014, in Los Angeles. At Sony Pictures, people sit down at their desks. They look at their computers. A red skeleton stares back at them. Words crawl across the screen. Hacked by GOP. [slowly] Then a warning. "This is just a beginning." Within hours, the computers go dark. One of Hollywood's biggest movie studios is suddenly cut off. And the people behind that skeleton? They're only getting started.

scenes.label: A studio, and a comedy
scenes.narration: [calmly] To see why this happened, let's go back a few months. Sony Pictures is a giant Hollywood studio. It's part of Sony, the Japanese company that makes the PlayStation. Thousands of people work there. That year, the studio had a comedy ready for Christmas. It was called The Interview. In the movie, two Americans are sent to kill North Korea's leader, Kim Jong Un. In June 2014, North Korea called the film "an act of war." [softly] To them, this movie was not funny at all.

scenes.label: Thieves already inside
scenes.narration: [curious] But here's the strange part. The thieves were already inside. According to US investigators, the attackers spent at least two months secretly copying Sony's files. One person who claimed to speak for the hackers said it was closer to a year. And nobody at Sony noticed. Think of a burglar hiding in your attic for weeks. He quietly carries your things out the back door, one box at a time. Then, on November 21, he left a note.

visuals.at: claimed to speak for the hackers

scenes.label: An email nobody took seriously
scenes.narration: [cautiously] That Friday, an email landed in the inboxes of Sony's top bosses. Two of them were Michael Lynton, the company's chief executive, and Amy Pascal, who ran the movie side. The sender called itself God's Apostles. It asked for money. It warned that Sony would be "bombarded as a whole." [sighs] Most of them ignored it. Big companies get weird emails all the time. It looked like spam. Three days later, the skeleton showed up.

scenes.label: The wiper goes off
scenes.narration: [serious] Now, back to that Monday. The skeleton was just the start. Behind it was something called a wiper. That's a kind of computer virus that doesn't steal things. It erases them. It wipes a computer so clean that it won't work anymore. [slowly] According to the FBI, thousands of Sony's computers were knocked out. Laptops, desktops, the big machines the whole studio ran on. All of it, frozen or gone. So how do you run a movie studio with no computers?

scenes.label: Hollywood goes back to paper
scenes.narration: [cautiously] The answer was: the old-fashioned way. People wrote things down with pens and paper. Sony handed out 190 BlackBerry phones so key staff could keep talking. Shops on the studio lot could only take cash. In public, Sony stayed very calm. It said it was looking into "an IT matter." That afternoon, Sony's top lawyer called in the FBI. A team from its Los Angeles cyber squad arrived the same day. They didn't know it yet, but the worst part hadn't even started.

scenes.label: The movies leak online
scenes.narration: [dramatically] The hackers called themselves the Guardians of Peace. And within days, they started putting Sony's secrets online for anyone to grab. First came the movies. Annie, a big holiday musical, showed up on pirate websites weeks before it hit theaters. Other new films leaked too. Later, a script for the next James Bond movie, Spectre, got out. For a studio, that's like a bank losing the cash in its vault. But the next leak hurt real people.

visuals.at: losing the cash in its vault

scenes.label: 47,000 Social Security numbers
scenes.narration: [serious] The hackers didn't just take movies. They took files about the people who worked there. Salaries. Details about their families. Even some medical information. By early December, news reports said about 47,000 Social Security numbers were out in the open. [slowly] That's about a packed Major League ballpark. Every seat holds someone whose private life just got dumped online. [sighs] Many were regular office workers, not movie stars. Soon, former workers sued Sony. And then the emails came out.

scenes.label: When the emails came out
scenes.narration: [cautiously] Years of private emails between Sony's most powerful people were suddenly out there. Reporters read them. Then they wrote about them. Some emails were just gossip about movie stars. Some were much worse. Amy Pascal and a famous producer, Scott Rudin, had to say sorry in public. Their emails about President Obama were called racially insensitive. No backup can un-leak an email. And the hackers still hadn't said clearly what they wanted.

scenes.label: A threat aimed at moviegoers
scenes.narration: [ominously] On December 16, they finally said it. For the first time, they named The Interview. They threatened the New York premiere, just two days away. And they threatened the Christmas Day release. The message told people to remember September 11, 2001. [slowly] This wasn't about stolen files anymore. Now the threat was aimed at regular people buying a movie ticket. Theater owners had to decide fast. Was a comedy worth the risk?

scenes.label: The movie disappears
scenes.narration: [nervous] One by one, the big theater chains backed out. Regal. AMC. Cinemark. Soon, all five of the biggest chains said no. So on December 17, Sony canceled the Christmas release. That same day, US officials told reporters that North Korea was "centrally involved." Michael Lynton later said the theaters left Sony no choice. "This was not our decision," he said. A group of hackers had just pulled a Hollywood movie out of American theaters.

scenes.label: The FBI names a country
scenes.narration: [serious] On December 19, the FBI made it official. "The North Korean government is responsible for these actions," it said. Agents pointed to clues. Parts of the code looked like older North Korean attacks. And internet addresses tied to North Korea had talked to the virus. That same day, President Obama held his year-end press conference. He said Sony had "made a mistake" by pulling the film. He didn't want "some dictator" deciding what Americans could see. [deep voice] "We will respond," he said.

scenes.label: Christmas on YouTube
scenes.narration: [curious] Then Sony changed its mind. On December 24, it put The Interview online, on YouTube, Google Play and Xbox. And on Christmas Day, a few hundred small, independent theaters showed it after all. People rushed to watch. Online, the movie made more than $40 million. Still, it lost money. And the hack cost Sony about $41 million by the end of March 2015. Meanwhile, on January 2, 2015, the US punished North Korea with new sanctions. Those are rules that block money and trade.

scenes.label: A name, four years later
scenes.narration: [slowly] After that, the case went quiet for years. Then came September 6, 2018. That day, the Justice Department charged a North Korean programmer named Park Jin Hyok. Prosecutors say he worked for a fake company. They say it was really a front for North Korea's military spies. They also accuse his team of much more. Stealing $81 million from a bank in Bangladesh. And WannaCry, a 2017 attack that froze computers in British hospitals. [softly] Park is still wanted. The charges are only accusations.

visuals.query: Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice Building
Park Jin Hyok FBI wanted poster

scenes.label: What the skeleton changed
scenes.narration: [reflective] So what did that skeleton change? At Sony, Amy Pascal stepped down as head of the studio in early 2015. Thousands of workers had watched their private details spread online. And every company learned a hard lesson. A hack isn't only about stolen data. It can wipe out machines. It can hurt ordinary workers. It can even decide which movie you get to see. [softly] All because of a comedy. If you like true stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

visuals.at: which movie you get to see

facts.claim: On November 24, 2014 Sony learned of the hack when malware made employee computers inoperable; Guardians of Peace released stolen data.
In June 2014 North Korea called The Interview, a comedy about killing Kim Jong Un, an 'act of war' and warned of retaliation.

Defacement read 'Hacked By #GOP' with 'We've already warned you, and this is just a beginning' and a deadline of November 24, 11:00 PM GMT.

A scarlet skeleton was displayed; employees worked with pens and paper; Sony issued 190 BlackBerrys; lot shops took only cash; Sony said 'We are investigating an IT matter'; FBI LA cyber squad arrived the same afternoon.
On November 21, 2014 'God'sApstls' emailed Lynton, Pascal and three other executives demanding 'monetary compensation'; most ignored it.
US investigators said attackers spent at least two months copying files; a claimant said up to a year; hackers claimed 100+ TB, not verified.
The attackers used a variant of the Shamoon wiper malware.

FBI: the attack rendered thousands of SPE's computers inoperable; 'the North Korean government is responsible for these actions'; 'deeply concerned about the destructive nature of this attack on a private sector entity.'
Leaked unreleased films included Annie, Mr. Turner and Still Alice; the Spectre screenplay leaked; salaries and future plans exposed.
About 47,000 unique Social Security numbers were exposed; four lawsuits filed by former employees in December 2014.
Amy Pascal and Scott Rudin apologized after racially insensitive emails about Obama leaked.
On December 16, 2014 the group named The Interview and threatened the December 18 New York premiere and December 25 release.
The Interview was planned for about 3,500 screens; the five major chains declined; Sony canceled on December 17; Lynton: 'This was not our decision.'
Obama said Sony 'made a mistake', warned against letting 'some dictator' control free speech, and said 'We will respond.'
About 300 mostly independent theaters showed the film on Christmas; online release December 24 on Google Play, Xbox Video and YouTube.
The Interview earned more than $40 million digitally and $12 million in theaters against a $65 million investment; hack out-of-pocket costs $41 million through March.
US imposed additional sanctions on North Korea on January 2, 2015.
On September 6, 2018 DOJ unsealed charges against Park Jin Hyok of Chosun Expo, affiliated with Lab 110; linked to Sony, $81 million Bangladesh Bank theft and WannaCry; Wray quote.
Tom Rothman replaced Amy Pascal in February 2015.
The November 21 email warned 'Sony Pictures will be bombarded as a whole'; the December 16 message invoked 'Remember the 11th of September 2001'.
FBI evidence: similarities in code, encryption and deletion methods to known North Korean attacks; IP addresses tied to North Korean infrastructure communicated with addresses hardcoded in the wiper.

seo.youtube_title: How Sony Pictures Got Hacked: The True Story Behind The Interview
seo.youtube_description:
How was Sony Pictures hacked? This is the true story of the 2014 Sony hack, told from start to finish in plain English.
A red skeleton, wiped computers, leaked movies, and a threat that pulled a Hollywood comedy out of theaters.

On November 24, 2014, workers at Sony Pictures turned on their computers and saw a red skeleton and the words "Hacked by GOP." The hackers had been inside for weeks. Their virus wiped thousands of computers. Then a group called the Guardians of Peace started leaking new movies, private emails and about 47,000 Social Security numbers.

When the hackers threatened theaters showing The Interview, the big chains backed out and Sony canceled the Christmas release. The FBI said North Korea was behind it. President Obama said Sony made a mistake. In 2018, the Justice Department charged a North Korean programmer, Park Jin Hyok. He is accused, not convicted.
